title: Text embeddings and rerankers: how search finds meaning in two passes
summary: How search finds documents that mean what you meant: from BM25 and the vocabulary problem, through sentence embeddings and contrastive dense retrieval, to cross-encoder and LLM rerankers, late interaction, and the measured limits of single-vector embeddings.

topics: deep dive: text embeddings and rerankers — how search finds meaning
concepts_taught: text embeddings for search: bi-encoders place query and document in one vector space so closeness (cosine or dot product) stands in for meaning; document vectors are precomputed and searched approximately (HNSW), trained contrastively with in-batch and BM25 hard negatives (DPR) because similar is not the same as relevant

rerankers as the second pass: a cross-encoder reads query and passage together so attention spans both, which is sharper but cannot be precomputed, hence retrieve-then-rerank over a top-100/1000 candidate list; LLM listwise rerankers (RankGPT) and late interaction (ColBERT's per-token MaxSim) as the expensive and middle options

the limits of single-vector retrieval: BM25 stays a robust zero-shot baseline (BEIR), no embedding model dominates all tasks (MTEB), and embedding dimension bounds which top-k document sets are reachable at all (Weller et al.'s LIMIT), so hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion plus a reranker is the practical default
